=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Executive view

The Seller’s package materially shifts known risks to the Buyer while attempting to restrict the Buyer’s remedies. We should not accept the proposed “general regime”. The key pushbacks are:

1. **No completion until Bluefen consent and Riverlark debt/security issues are resolved.**
2. **Price protection for Riverlark, employee bonuses and other pre-completion liabilities.**
3. **Specific indemnities for the export/privacy incident, Ironquay IP, bonuses and tax.**
4. **Narrower disclosure and knowledge provisions.**
5. **Higher or uncapped protection for title, tax, IP and specific indemnities.**
6. **No blanket non-reliance, exclusive-remedy or limitation provisions.**

## Material issues

### 1. Bluefen consent — critical condition precedent

Bluefen represents approximately 30% of FY26 revenue. The disclosure confirms:

- no final written consent;
- conditions under clause 11.3 may remain unsatisfied; and
- the Seller proposes only “reasonable endeavours”.

That is inadequate. Written consent alone may not be sufficient if the associated conditions are outstanding. Completion should be conditional on:

- final unconditional written consent;
- satisfaction or waiver of every related condition;
- confirmation that Bluefen cannot terminate, reprice or materially alter the contract; and
- no material adverse change in the relationship.

If consent is not obtained by the long-stop date, the Buyer should be able to terminate or obtain a price reduction/holdback. The Seller should not be able to deem the condition satisfied.

### 2. Riverlark — inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free pricing

The facility is approximately **AUD 3.2 million**, remains outstanding, and no discharge is available. A release “following Completion” leaves the Buyer exposed to:

- debt repayment;
- secured creditor enforcement;
- security interests over Company assets;
- refinancing or release costs; and
- a potentially inaccurate debt-free/cash-free completion balance.

Require repayment and release before or simultaneously with Completion, supported by lender payoff and release documents. At minimum, retain the full amount plus a buffer in escrow or deduct it from the purchase price, with a Seller indemnity for all related liabilities.

### 3. Employee bonuses — undisclosed completion liability

The AUD 420,000 bonuses are triggered by Completion and may create payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. They are absent from the funds flow.

This is a direct economic cost of the transaction and should not be left to the Buyer. Require the Seller to:

- pay and discharge the bonuses and all on-costs before Completion; or
- deduct the full gross amount, including all employer charges, from the purchase price; and
- indemnify the Buyer and Company for any related claims.

The funds flow must expressly show the treatment.

### 4. Broad general disclosure

The proposed disclosure of the entire data room, accounts, registers and public records is too broad. It risks turning every document into a warranty exception, regardless of whether the issue was reasonably identifiable.

Require that disclosure be:

- specific, accurate and fairly disclosed;
- sufficiently detailed to identify the nature, scope and likely impact of the issue;
- limited to documents expressly indexed and actually accessible;
- subject to the Buyer’s warranties remaining true except for matters fairly disclosed; and
- not expanded by public registers or generic data-room disclosure.

The Seller’s reservation that nothing admits liability does not cure inadequate disclosure and should not override the SPA warranties.

### 5. Buyer knowledge provision

The proposal excludes claims for anything known by the Buyer or its advisers, including anything discoverable in the data room or public records. This is effectively a constructive-knowledge exclusion and could defeat much of the warranty package.

Limit the provision to:

- actual knowledge;
- of specifically named Buyer personnel;
- after reasonable internal inquiry; and
- excluding advisers’ inferred or constructive knowledge.

It should not apply to fraud, deliberate concealment, title, tax, specific indemnities, or matters inaccurately or incompletely disclosed.

### 6. Liability caps, baskets and time limits

The proposed general cap is **AUD 4.8 million**, only 20% of the purchase price. That may be insufficient given the known risks.

The AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 basket should not apply to:

- title and capacity;
- tax;
- IP;
- fraud or wilful misconduct;
- specific indemnities;
- debt-free/cash-free adjustments; or
- claims relating to the known Bluefen, Riverlark, bonus and privacy matters.

The Buyer should seek:

- title and capacity liability up to at least the purchase price, or uncapped;
- separate, higher limits for tax and IP;
- uncapped fraud and intentional concealment;
- specific indemnities outside the general cap and basket; and
- a true “tipping” basket or, preferably, no basket for material known risks.

An 18-month general warranty period is short. Tax claims should survive for the relevant statutory period, title claims should survive indefinitely or for a substantially longer period, and specific indemnities should continue until the relevant matter is finally resolved.

### 7. Blanket limitations, non-reliance and exclusive remedy

Applying these provisions to “all Claims” is unacceptable. They could remove remedies for:

- breach of the SPA;
- debt or price adjustments;
- specific indemnities;
- fraud and misleading conduct;
- equitable relief;
- statutory rights; and
- post-completion obligations.

Preserve all contractual, statutory, equitable and common-law remedies, subject only to agreed limitations for ordinary warranty claims. The Buyer should also retain the right to seek injunctions, specific performance, debt recovery and enforcement of indemnities.

### 8. Ironquay IP

The disclosure indicates AUD 180,000 remains open and that transfer of SOW3 materials depends on payment of every SOW3 fee. The existing indemnity, limited to one payment, is too narrow.

Require:

- evidence of the outstanding amount and payment status;
- transfer/assignment of all relevant IP and project materials at or before Completion;
- confirmation of chain of title and third-party rights; and
- a specific indemnity covering payment, failure to obtain ownership, infringement, loss of use and related costs.

Payment should not be made without obtaining the required IP transfer.

### 9. Export/privacy incident

The incident potentially concerns approximately 1,240 records and remains unresolved. The Seller’s characterisation as “preliminary” does not eliminate the risk of regulatory notification, affected-person notification, remediation, customer claims or reputational loss.

Require a dedicated indemnity covering:

- investigation and forensic costs;
- legal and regulatory costs;
- notifications and remediation;
- customer and individual claims;
- monitoring and credit-protection measures, if required; and
- penalties or other losses to the extent legally recoverable.

The Seller should preserve evidence, cooperate fully and provide continuing updates. This risk should sit outside the general cap, basket and knowledge exclusion.

### 10. Supplier renewals

The three AUD 110,000 renewals should not be accepted as ordinary-course costs without reviewing their terms. They may represent unavoidable post-completion commitments or related-party arrangements.

Require disclosure of:

- renewal dates and termination rights;
- accrued or committed amounts;
- pricing and volume obligations;
- related-party connections; and
- whether the commitments were entered into in the ordinary course.

Any pre-completion liability should be paid by the Seller or reflected in the price/working-capital adjustment.

### 11. Lease and Mossvale arrangements

The Seller’s disclosure does not establish that consent is unnecessary. It merely says the documents do not describe consent as required.

Require confirmation from the relevant counterparties or legal analysis demonstrating that:

- no consent or waiver is required;
- no termination or default right is triggered;
- no notification has adverse consequences; and
- the arrangements continue unchanged after Completion.

If consent is legally or commercially required, make it a completion condition.

### 12. Title and share ownership

The share register is useful but not sufficient evidence of clean title. Require warranties that:

- Harbourglass owns the shares legally and beneficially;
- the shares are fully paid;
- the shares are free of security interests, options and other encumbrances;
- there are no agreements affecting ownership or voting;
- all corporate approvals have been obtained; and
- the Company has no undisclosed issued or convertible securities.

Title should be a fundamental warranty with enhanced survival and liability protection.

### 13. Tax and IP warranties

The Seller’s statement that tax and IP are “settled” is not an agreement. The Buyer should retain robust warranties and specific indemnities for:

- pre-Completion tax liabilities;
- payroll tax, superannuation and employment on-costs;
- GST and transaction taxes;
- IP ownership and employee/contractor assignments;
- infringement;
- open-source compliance; and
- loss of rights in customer or development materials.

## Recommended negotiating position

### Must-have

- Bluefen consent and conditions satisfied before Completion.
- Riverlark repaid and security released before or at Completion.
- Bonus liabilities paid by Seller or deducted with all on-costs.
- Specific indemnities for privacy, Ironquay, Riverlark, bonuses and tax.
- No blanket constructive-knowledge exclusion.
- No general disclosure of the entire data room without fair-disclosure qualification.
- Fundamental, tax, IP and indemnity claims excluded from ordinary caps, baskets and 18-month limits.
- Preservation of fraud, statutory, equitable and contractual remedies.

### Strongly preferred

- Higher general cap than 20%.
- Longer warranty survival periods.
- Counterparty confirmations for lease and Mossvale.
- Detailed review and treatment of supplier renewals.
- Completion escrow/retention for unresolved risks.
- Expressly itemised funds flow.

### Overall recommendation

Treat the Seller update as a risk-allocation proposal, not a balanced compromise. The known liabilities are sufficiently material that the Buyer should either obtain the protections above or demand a corresponding price reduction and substantial escrow.
